title: Cities of the Silk Road
intro: For centuries, Samarkand and Bukhara were among the busiest trading cities on the famous routes between China and Europe.

passage: For more than a thousand years, a huge network of trade routes connected China with the Mediterranean Sea. Today we call it the Silk Road, although this name was only invented in the nineteenth century by a German geographer. In fact, it was never a single road. It was a collection of paths across deserts, mountains and grasslands, and very few traders ever travelled along the whole route. Instead, goods were passed from one merchant to another, and from one city to the next.

Silk was the most famous product that moved west, because for centuries only the Chinese knew how to make it. Rich people in Rome and Persia were willing to pay very high prices for this soft, shiny material. But many other goods were also exchanged, such as spices, glass, horses, paper, gold and precious stones. Merchants usually travelled together in long caravans of camels, which could carry heavy loads and survive for days without water. The journey was slow and difficult, and thieves and bad weather were a constant threat.

In the middle of this network lay the cities of Central Asia, and two of the most important were Samarkand and Bukhara. Their location made them ideal places for travellers to rest, buy food and do business. The people of Sogdiana, the region around Samarkand, became especially well known as skilled merchants. They spoke many languages and set up communities in towns as far away as China. Some historians believe that, for several centuries, Sogdian was the main language of trade along the eastern part of the route.

Bukhara grew rich in a similar way. Travellers stayed in caravanserais, large buildings with a courtyard in the middle where both people and animals could sleep safely. Later, covered markets with domed roofs were built at busy crossroads, and each one specialised in particular goods, such as hats, jewellery or money exchange. Several of these markets can still be visited today. The tall Kalyan Minaret, which was built in the twelfth century, is said to have helped travellers find the city across the flat desert.

However, the Silk Road was about much more than buying and selling. Ideas, religions, music and inventions travelled along it too. According to a popular story, the secret of making paper reached Samarkand from China in the eighth century, and Samarkand paper later became famous across the Islamic world. Scholars in the region also made important discoveries in science. In the fifteenth century, the ruler Ulugh Beg built an observatory in Samarkand, where astronomers produced remarkably accurate tables of the stars.

From the fifteenth and sixteenth centuries, European ships began to carry goods by sea, which was cheaper and faster, and the old land routes slowly declined. Yet the great cities did not disappear. Today, both Samarkand and Bukhara are UNESCO World Heritage Sites, and thousands of tourists come every year to admire their blue domes and ancient streets. Modern projects that aim to connect Asia and Europe by railway have even been described as a 'new Silk Road'. It seems that this old idea of connection is still alive.

mcq.q: Why did people in Rome and Persia pay so much for silk?
options: It was difficult to carry across the desert.
For a long time, only the Chinese could produce it.
Only rulers were allowed to wear it.

mcq.q: What was special about the covered markets in Bukhara?
options: Each one sold a particular kind of product.
They were built in the desert outside the city.
Travellers and their camels could sleep inside them.

mcq.q: According to paragraph F, why did the land routes become less important?
options: The cities along them were destroyed.
Transporting goods by ship cost less and took less time.
